triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: material provision for widows and orphans
triples.rationale: Judas's people allocate part of the spoils to the maltreated, widows and orphans before dividing the remainder among their households. Deuteronomy directs stored produce to recipients including the orphan and widow so that they may eat and be filled. Both include these vulnerable groups in the distribution of community resources; battlefield spoil is not identified as the prescribed tithe.
triples.source_text: After the Sabbath they gave a share of the spoils to the maltreated, the widows and the orphans, and divided the rest among themselves and their children.

target_units.text: After three years you shall bring forth all the tithe of your produce; in that year you shall lay it up within your cities.

And the Levite, for he has neither portion nor inheritance with you, and the sojourner, and the orphan, and the widow within your cities shall come, and eat, and be filled; that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works which you do.

triples.relationship: Wisdom parallel: insolence preceding a fall
triples.rationale: Antiochus continues in arrogance, orders greater speed, and suffers a bodily fall from his rushing chariot. Proverbs places insolence before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall. The proverb supplies a moral pattern for the narrative's explicit sequence of persistent haughtiness and collapse, without predicting this particular accident.
triples.source_text: Yet he did not cease his haughtiness at all, but was still filled with arrogance, breathing fire in his anger against the Jews and ordering the journey hastened. He happened to fall from the chariot as it rushed along, and in the severe fall all the members of his body were wrenched.

target_units.text: Insolence leads before ruin, and evil-mindedness before a fall.

triples.relationship: Literary parallel: star-reaching royal arrogance brought low
triples.rationale: Antiochus's imagined reach to heaven's stars is set against his body's intolerable smell. Isaiah's lament over Babylon's king similarly opposes the wish to rise above the stars and resemble the Most High to descent, decay and worms. Both expose a ruler's heavenly pretensions through bodily degradation; they concern different kings, and Isaiah does not describe Antiochus's transport difficulty.
triples.source_text: No one could carry the man who a little earlier thought he could touch the stars of heaven, because of the unbearable weight of his smell.

target_units.text: Your glory went down to Hades, your abundant gladness. They will spread decay beneath you, and your covering is a worm.
How the dawn-bearer who rises in the morning fell from heaven! The one dispatching to all the nations was shattered to earth.
You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above heaven’s stars, and sit on a high mountain, upon the high mountains toward the north.
I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’
But now you will descend to Hades and to the earth’s foundations.

triples.relationship: Wisdom parallel: a belated appeal denied after persistent rejection
triples.rationale: Antiochus makes vows amid the judgment following his continued arrogance, but the narrator says that the Master will no longer have mercy on him. Wisdom warns those who repeatedly rejected her counsel that their calls in calamity will go unanswered. The comparison concerns the rejected late appeal; Wisdom's speech is not attributed directly to Antiochus's addressee, and his vows are not treated as successful repentance.
triples.source_text: The defiled man made vows to the Master who would no longer have mercy on him, speaking in this way:

target_units.text: Since I kept calling and you did not obey, and kept extending words and you paid no attention,
but you were making my counsels ineffective and disobeyed my reproofs,
therefore I too will laugh at your ruin and exult when destruction comes to you,
and when sudden tumult reaches you and overthrow arrives like a storm, when affliction and siege come upon you, or when destruction comes to you.
For when you call upon me, I will not listen to you; evil people will seek me and will not find me,
for they hated wisdom and did not choose the fear of the Lord,
nor did they want to attend to my counsels, but they were sneering at my reproofs.
Therefore they will eat the fruits of their own way and be filled with their own ungodliness.

triples.relationship: Narrative comparison: humbled kings and public proclamation of God
triples.rationale: Antiochus promises to travel through inhabited places proclaiming God's might. Nebuchadnezzar's letters actually summon nations to praise God and announce His great deeds after the king's restoration. Both connect royal humiliation with proposed or enacted public witness to God's power; Antiochus's vow is not a reported fulfillment or identified with Nebuchadnezzar's letters.
triples.source_text: Besides these things, he would become a Jew and go through every inhabited place, proclaiming God’s might.

target_units.text: King Nebuchadnezzar wrote a circular letter to all the nations in every place, to the countries and all languages dwelling in every country, from generation to generation: “Praise the Lord, the God of heaven, and gloriously bring Him sacrifice and offering. I, king of kings, gloriously give thanks to Him, because He has dealt with me in this way: on that very day He seated me upon my throne; I regained my authority and my kingdom among my people, and my greatness was restored to me.”

“King Nebuchadnezzar to all nations, all countries, and all who dwell in them: May peace be multiplied to you at every time. Now I will explain to you the deeds that the great God has done with me. It pleased me to demonstrate to you and to your learned experts that there is a God, and His wonders are great; His kingship is an everlasting kingship, His authority from generation to generation.” He sent letters concerning everything that had happened to him in his kingdom to all the nations under his kingship.

triples.relationship: Narrative parallel: confronting a foe whose speech defies God
triples.rationale: The young men assault the wall in anger at the defenders' blasphemies. David likewise resolves to confront the foreigner who defied the living God's battle line and remove Israel's disgrace, trusting in the Lord's rescue. Both relate courageous confrontation to the enemy's insulting speech; David is not assigned the young men's stated fury or their siege tactics.
triples.source_text: As the fifth day dawned, twenty young men of Maccabeus’s company, burning with anger because of the blasphemies, attacked the wall courageously and cut down whoever they met with a beast-like fury.

target_units.text: Your servant struck both bear and lion. The uncircumcised foreigner will be like one of them. Shall I not go and strike him and remove disgrace from Israel today? For who is this uncircumcised man who has defied the battle line of the living God?
The Lord, who rescued me from the lion’s paw and the bear’s paw, will rescue me from this uncircumcised foreigner’s hand.” Saul said to David, “Go, and the Lord will be with you.”

triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: sharing the danger of brothers at war
triples.rationale: Maccabeus takes up arms and urges others to share the danger and help their brothers. Moses challenges Gad and Reuben against remaining behind while their brothers go to war and against discouraging Israel's advance. Both insist that the conflict of one's brothers calls for participation, with Judas's eager response differing from the tribes' initial request.
triples.source_text: Maccabeus himself was the first to take up his weapons. He urged the others to share the danger with him and help their brothers. Together and eagerly they set out.

target_units.text: And Moses said to the sons of Gad and sons of Reuben: Your brothers are going to war, and will you sit here?
And why do you turn aside the minds of the sons of Israel so that they do not cross into the land that the Lord is giving them?

triples.relationship: Imagery parallel: confidence in divine aid against a wall
triples.rationale: Blessing God, Judas's company grows ready to pierce even iron walls; the psalmist declares that by God he will cross over a wall. Both use overcoming a wall to express confidence in divine aid amid military danger. Piercing and crossing are distinct images, and the Maccabean statement is readiness rather than a report of an actual breached iron wall.
triples.source_text: Together they all blessed the merciful God and grew strong in spirit, ready to pierce not only human beings but the fiercest wild animals and iron walls.

target_units.text: For by Thee I will be rescued from a raiding band, and by my God I will cross over a wall.

triples.relationship: Literary parallel: Judas's warfare described with lion imagery
triples.rationale: The company with Maccabeus rushes upon the enemy like lions. The praise of Judas in 1 Maccabees likewise likens his deeds to a lion and a young lion roaring over prey. The correspondence is martial lion imagery associated with Judas's warfare, not proof that the praise identifies this particular engagement or its casualty figures.
triples.source_text: Rushing like lions upon the enemy, they struck down eleven thousand of them and sixteen hundred horsemen; they forced all the rest to flee.

target_units.text: In his deeds he was like a lion, like a young lion roaring over prey.

triples.relationship: Narrative parallel: an apparently welcoming invitation conceals violence
triples.rationale: The people of Joppa invite their Jewish neighbors onto boats as if no hostility existed, before the drowning described next. Ishmael similarly invites arriving mourners to come to Gedaliah, whose killing is still unknown, and slaughters them after they enter. Both invitations conceal lethal intentions from their recipients; the victims, locations and means of killing differ.
triples.source_text: The people of Joppa committed this great impiety. They invited the Jews living among them to board boats that they had provided, with their wives and children, as though there were no hostility toward them,

target_units.text: On the second day after he struck Gedaliah, when no one knew,
eighty men came from Shechem, Salem, and Samaria, with shaved beards and torn clothes, beating themselves, carrying grain offerings and frankincense to bring to the Lord’s house.
Ishmael went out to meet them. They were walking and weeping, and he said to them, Come in to Gedaliah.
When they entered the middle of the city, he slaughtered them into the cistern.

triples.relationship: Thematic contrast: seeking advantage in Judah's disaster
triples.rationale: The nations joining Nicanor expect the Jews' misfortunes to become their own successes. Obadiah condemns standing with Jerusalem's attackers and forbids rejoicing over Judah's destruction or joining the attack. This brings the hostile expectation of gain alongside the prophetic prohibition of benefiting from Judah's calamity; the nations in Judea are not identified as Obadiah's Idumea.
triples.source_text: The nations in Judea who had driven Judas into exile joined Nicanor in crowds, thinking the Jews’ misfortunes and disasters would become their own successes.

target_units.text: From the day you stood opposed, on the day foreigners took his strength captive and strangers entered his gates and cast lots over Jerusalem, you too were like one of them.
Do not look on your brother’s day, on the day of strangers; do not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction; do not speak boastfully on the day of affliction.

Do not enter the gates of peoples on the day of their suffering. You, too, must not look on their assembly on the day of their destruction, and do not join in attacking their strength on the day of their destruction.

triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: fatherhood as an image of public care
triples.rationale: Razis is called a father of the Jews because of his goodwill toward his fellow citizens. Job describes his assistance to the orphan, widow and powerless and calls himself a father to the powerless. In both, fatherhood expresses care beyond a biological household; Job's particular acts are not ascribed to Razis.
triples.source_text: A certain Razis, one of Jerusalem’s elders, was reported to Nicanor: a man who loved his fellow citizens, was very well spoken of, and because of his goodwill was called a father of the Jews.

target_units.text: For I rescued a poor person from a powerful man’s hand and helped an orphan who had no helper.
May the blessing of the perishing come upon me, and a widow’s mouth blessed me.
I had clothed myself with righteousness, and I wrapped myself in justice like a double cloak.
I was an eye for the blind and a foot for the lame.
I was a father to the powerless, and I traced out a case I did not know.

triples.relationship: Rhetorical parallel: an earthly ruler questions divine authority
triples.rationale: Nicanor asks whether a Sovereign in heaven commanded Sabbath observance, setting up his own competing earthly command. Pharaoh similarly asks who the Lord is that he should obey His voice and release Israel for a feast. Both questions challenge the divine authority invoked to limit a ruler's demands; the required observances and historical conflicts differ.
triples.source_text: The thrice-accursed man asked whether there was a Sovereign in heaven who had commanded the observance of the Sabbath day.

target_units.text: Afterward Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said, “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: ‘Let My people go so that they may hold a feast for Me in the wilderness.’”
Pharaoh said, “Who is He, that I should obey His voice and let the sons of Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.”

triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: leaders strengthen troops through words of divine help
triples.rationale: Judas arms his people with encouraging words more than confidence in shields and lances, in a context of expecting help from the Almighty. Hezekiah likewise tells his people that the Lord will save and fight for them, contrasting divine help with the enemy's arms of flesh, and they take courage from his words. The connection is the effect of spoken encouragement grounded in divine help, not an identification of Judas's dream with Hezekiah's speech.
triples.source_text: Arming each of them with the encouragement of good words more than with the security of shields and lances, he also related a trustworthy dream, a kind of waking vision, and gladdened them all.

target_units.text: He appointed commanders of war over the people, and they gathered to him in the square at the gate of the ravine. He spoke to their hearts, saying,
“Be strong and act courageously. Do not be terrified before the king of Assyria or before the entire nation with him, because more are with us than with him.
With him are arms of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God, to save and to fight our war.” The people took courage from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.

deferred_source_units.source_text: He urged him to marry and have children. Judas married, settled down and shared in ordinary life.
deferred_source_units.reason: Jeremiah 36:5-7 was actually checked as a possible comparison for marriage, children and ordinary settled life. Its instructions to deportees do not establish Judas's marriage or a distinct literary connection beyond common domestic actions. No sufficiently particular supported match was retained; no spouse, children or historical identity is inferred.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: He urged him to marry and have children. Judas married, settled down and shared in ordinary life.
unresolved_candidates.reason: Both passages concern marriage and children alongside settled life, but Jeremiah commands deportees to build homes, plant gardens and seek their land's peace, while Nicanor urges Judas to marry during their friendship. The common domestic actions alone were not retained as a sufficiently particular connection, and the passage supplies no independent details of Judas's family.

target_units.text: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits,
and take wives and beget sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands. Multiply and do not become fewer,
and seek the peace of the land where I deported you, and pray to the Lord for them, because in its peace you will have peace.
